opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a very natural reaction, and honestly, I'd be worried if people weren't cautious. Driving is one of the few everyday activities where we hand our lives over to something. For more than a century, the "something" has always been a human being we can see, talk to, and judge. When you get into a car with no one in the driver's seat, you're being asked to trust a system you can't see and don't fully understand. That's a big psychological leap.

There are a few layers to it. The first is the asymmetry in how we judge machines and people. Human drivers cause an enormous number of accidents every year, and society has more or less accepted that as the cost of mobility. But when an autonomous vehicle makes a mistake, even a minor one, it becomes headline news. We hold machines to a much higher standard, and in a way that's fair. If we're going to deploy this technology at scale, it shouldn't be just as good as an average human driver. It should be significantly safer, and it has to show that consistently.

The second layer is explainability. When a human driver brakes suddenly, you can ask why, and they'll tell you they saw a child or a dog. With an AI system, especially an end-to-end model, the decision process is much less transparent. People are uncomfortable with a black box making life-or-death decisions, so part of our job as technologists is to make these systems more interpretable and more predictable in their behavior.

The third layer is simply familiarity. Trust is built through experience, not through statistics on a slide. Almost everyone I know who has taken a ride in a robotaxi, including people who were very skeptical, gets nervous for the first few minutes and then gets bored. They start looking at their phone. That is the moment trust begins. So scale matters. The more cities you operate in, the more rides people take, and the more real-world miles the system accumulates, the faster acceptance grows. We've seen this with elevators, airplanes, and autopilot in aviation. Each of them was frightening at first, and each became normal.

There's also a social dimension we shouldn't ignore. Some of the hesitation isn't about safety. It's about jobs, about who is accountable when something goes wrong, and about how these vehicles share the road with human drivers. Those are legitimate concerns, and technology companies can't solve them alone. They need regulators, cities, insurers, and the public at the table.

So my view is that the hesitation isn't a barrier to resent. It's a signal. It tells us that safety has to come first, transparency has to improve, and deployment has to be gradual and responsible. If we do that well, I believe that within the next decade, people will look back and find it strange that we ever let humans drive, tired, distracted, or texting, at sixty miles an hour.

r001.rationale: The response links hesitation to unfamiliarity with driverless cars, describing trust as something that grows through experience and comparing the technology with initially frightening innovations.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the hesitation is very natural, and honestly I don't see it as a problem with the public. It's a problem of trust, and trust is built differently from capability.

When I was at Baidu leading Apollo, our engineers would show me the numbers. Disengagement rates, miles per intervention, accident rates per hundred million kilometers. On almost every metric the system was already safer than the average human driver in the test zones. But people don't experience statistics. They experience that one video of a robotaxi stuck in an intersection in Wuhan, or the moment the car brakes hard for no reason they can see. A human driver who makes a mistake, we forgive, because we understand why. A machine that makes a mistake, we don't forgive, because we don't understand it. That asymmetry is the core of it.

There is also a question of who is responsible. When a person drives, the accountability is clear. With Apollo Go, is it Baidu, the city, the operator sitting remotely, the algorithm? Until that chain is legible to ordinary people, there will be unease, no matter how good the driving is.

And then there is a social layer that engineers tend to underestimate. In China there are several million ride-hailing and taxi drivers. When Apollo Go expanded in Wuhan, the debate was not really about safety, it was about jobs. The technology arrived faster than the social conversation around it. I always say the last ten percent of autonomous driving is not technical, it is regulatory, it is insurance, it is public acceptance. That ten percent can take longer than the first ninety.

So my view is, the capability is necessary but not sufficient. What moves acceptance is boring things: operating for years without a serious incident, transparent reporting, clear liability rules, and letting people ride it for themselves. Every person who takes an Apollo Go ride and feels the car is calm and predictable becomes an advocate. Familiarity does the work that benchmarks cannot. We saw the same curve with elevators, with airplanes. Nobody worries now about an elevator without an operator. In ten years I think people will find it strange that we ever worried about this.

r001.rationale: The response links unease to Apollo Go’s arrival outpacing public discussion and says familiarity helps build acceptance, communicating that its relative novelty contributes to hesitation.

astra-6.text:
I think the hesitation is understandable. Riding in a car without a driver is a very different experience from hearing that the technology performs well. People are putting their safety in the hands of a system they may not understand, and they want to know: Can it handle an unexpected situation? What happens if something goes wrong? Who is responsible?

So driving capability is necessary, but it is not enough. Trust has to be earned through consistent performance, transparent safety information, and clear accountability. Personal experience matters, too. A ride that feels unfamiliar at first can become reassuring when the vehicle behaves predictably and safely.

We should take those concerns seriously. The goal is to demonstrate, over time, that this service is safe, reliable, and useful in people’s daily lives.

r001.rationale: The response links hesitation to the driverless ride being a very different, unfamiliar experience for the public.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the hesitation is understandable. Riding in a car without a human driver requires a different kind of trust. People are asking not only, “Can it drive well?” but also, “What happens when something unexpected occurs? Who is responsible if something goes wrong?” Those are legitimate questions.

For Apollo Go, driving capability is essential, but public acceptance also depends on transparency, consistent performance, and experience. People need to understand the system’s limits and see how it handles difficult situations. Trust has to be earned over time through safe, reliable service. We should listen to those concerns and address them patiently.

r001.rationale: The response explains hesitation through trust, uncertainty about unexpected events, and accountability, but does not attribute it to Apollo Go’s relative novelty.
